items.prompt: A report misses a deadline with no warning. What kind of signal is the missed deadline?
choices: A leading signal, because it warns of trouble still to come ahead
A lagging signal, confirming that the trouble has already happened
A background signal, because it says little about the person involved
items.explanation: A missed deadline is the end of the chain, so it confirms a problem rather than predicting one.

items.prompt: Which of these is a leading signal?
choices: A deadline passing unmet
A release going out late
Updates getting vaguer
items.explanation: Vaguer updates show up before output suffers, which is what makes them leading.

items.prompt: Why is the missed deadline the worst place to learn about a problem?
choices: It is the latest point at which any problem can be found out
It is the only point at which anyone finds out about trouble
It unfairly blames the wrong person for what went wrong later
items.explanation: By the deadline the cause has been building for a while, so the chance to help early is gone.

items.prompt: What does a lagging signal do?
choices: Predicts a problem that has not yet started
Confirms a problem that has already happened
Measures how happy someone is at work generally
items.explanation: Lagging means after the fact.

items.prompt: Report B stayed quiet for three weeks. When was the problem first visible?
choices: On the morning of the missed deadline
Only after Report B eventually explained it all
Weeks earlier, as quiet changes in behavior
items.explanation: The changes were observable the whole time; nobody was watching for them.

items.prompt: Which sentence best describes most early signs of struggle?
choices: They are mostly absences, like fewer messages
They are loud events that demand attention right away
They are formal complaints sent to the manager directly
items.explanation: Withdrawal is quiet, which is exactly why it is easy to miss.

items.prompt: A manager only reviews task status. What will they mostly see?
choices: Leading signals, well before output suffers at all
Lagging signals, after the trouble has landed
Nothing, because status never shows trouble
items.explanation: Task status reflects output, which moves late.

items.prompt: Report A flagged a blocker in week 2. Why was the manager not surprised by A's lateness?
choices: A is simply a more skilled worker than B is
A finished all of the work earlier than B did
It was named while there was time to plan
items.explanation: Early disclosure turned a lagging surprise into a known risk.

items.prompt: A manager says 'if something were wrong, the missed deadline would tell me.' What is the flaw in that plan?
choices: The deadline is an unreliable signal, so it often hides real problems completely
The deadline only matters for reports, so managers should watch their own work too
The deadline is the last signal, so it reports after the cost is paid
The deadline arrives too early, so it flags problems that would have resolved themselves
items.explanation: The plan is consistent but late: it detects every problem, just after the cost has been paid.
items.reference:
Where each signal sits
quiet behavior change: leading
quality slips: in between
missed deadline: lagging, last
Why: a lagging signal confirms a problem that already happened, so waiting for it means finding out as late as possible.
items.learnMore:
Lagging vs. leading

A missed deadline confirms damage already done. Quiet changes in behavior come earlier and give a manager time to help.

Common mistake

Treating the missed deadline as the moment the problem started, when it was only the moment it became visible.
items.reflection: Think of a project that failed visibly. What small thing changed weeks before anyone said anything?

items.prompt: Which observation is a leading signal rather than a lagging one?
choices: A report whose pull request was merged three days late last sprint
A report who used to ask questions now asks none for two weeks
A report whose last release had to be rolled back by the team
A report whose quarterly goals were marked as missed in review
items.explanation: Only the first is behavior before an outcome; the others are outcomes.

choices: Information reached the manager sooner from the first
The first report was less responsible
The second report slipped more, so the manager felt more surprise
Both slips were equal, so surprise comes from the manager's mood
items.explanation: Same lagging event, different amounts of leading information.

choices: As a lagging signal, since the quality problem is already present
As a pure leading signal, since no tangible output has been touched
As noise, since the date is not at risk
As in-between: output is hit, but no deadline has moved yet
items.explanation: Quality sits between withdrawal and a missed date: damage has begun but is not yet consequential.

items.prompt: One report gives a shorter standup update this week and nothing else changes. What is the right read?
choices: Note it, but do not treat it as proof yet
Treat it as a confirmed sign of a crisis
Ignore it forever, since it can never matter
items.explanation: One signal has many ordinary explanations.

items.prompt: What turns a few signals into a pattern worth acting on?
choices: They each happen once in different people
They persist or stack together in one person
They happen only on the final day of a sprint
items.explanation: Persistence or accumulation is what separates a pattern from noise.

items.prompt: What do 'camera off more often' and 'slower replies' usually share?
choices: They both prove the person dislikes the team
They both mean the person is working harder than ever
They can both reflect withdrawal or overload
items.explanation: Different surfaces, similar possible causes.

items.prompt: Whose baseline should you compare a report's behavior against?
choices: Their own earlier, normal behavior
The team's most talkative person
An average of every team in the company
items.explanation: A signal is a change from this person's normal.

items.prompt: A usually chatty report goes quiet for two weeks. Why is that informative?
choices: Quiet people are always struggling people
It is a change from their own pattern
Chatty people should never go quiet
items.explanation: Change against baseline is the information.

items.prompt: Fewer questions asked can mean what?
choices: Always laziness, which needs no further thought
Always mastery, so the manager can fully relax
Confidence, or a belief asking no longer helps
items.explanation: The same behavior has more than one cause, which is why a pattern is needed.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest case for acting?
choices: Camera off, slow replies, short updates for weeks
One late reply on a busy Monday during a release
One skipped optional meeting during a holiday week, once
items.explanation: Several signals, same direction, sustained.

items.prompt: What is the danger of reacting to every single quiet day?
choices: You would miss every real signal that follows later on
Normal variation is treated as trouble
You would remove the need for any private conversation
items.explanation: Over-reacting is its own failure.

items.prompt: A report's updates got shorter on Monday. By Friday they are shorter again, replies are slower, and the camera has stayed off. What changed between Monday and Friday?
choices: The signals each became more severe, so one alone now proves trouble
Independent signals accumulated in the same person and direction
The week ended, so the manager's patience for quiet is simply used up
The report disclosed a struggle, which makes the earlier signals count
items.explanation: Nothing got louder; stacking independent signals is what makes coincidence a poor explanation.
items.reference:
One signal vs. a pattern
1 shorter update, 1 week: note it
same signal over several days: watch it
several signals, same direction: act
Why: a single signal has many ordinary explanations; persistence or accumulation in one person is what separates noise from a likely problem.
items.learnMore:
Pattern against the person's baseline

Signals matter relative to how this person normally behaves. A usually chatty report who goes quiet is informative; a naturally quiet one staying quiet is not.

Common mistake

Reading a single data point as proof, or comparing everyone against one team-wide idea of normal.
items.reflection: Think of someone you know well. What is their normal, and which change from it would you notice first?

items.prompt: Two reports both go quiet for a week. One is normally talkative, the other has always been reserved. Who is the stronger early-signal case?
choices: The talkative one, because quiet breaks their own baseline pattern
The reserved one, because quiet people hide their struggles most
Both equally, because a week of silence is the same everywhere
Neither, because a single week can never count for anything
items.explanation: Signals are relative to a person's own baseline, not to a team average.

As proof of a crisis, since three weeks is always fully conclusive
As irrelevant, since nothing about it is getting any worse over time
As more than one event, since persistence is itself a pattern
items.explanation: Persistence over time can carry the same weight as variety across signals.

Signals come in groups, which makes watching them pointless

Direct statements are the only evidence that carries any weight
items.explanation: Waiting for words means waiting past the weeks when the pattern was visible.

items.prompt: What is psychological safety?
choices: A belief that deadlines never slip
A rule that nobody may ever give negative feedback
That admitting a struggle brings support
items.explanation: It is about what the person expects to happen after speaking up.

items.prompt: In a low-safety team, what is a typical first response to 'how is it going?'
choices: A reflexive 'fine' answer
A detailed list of every blocker
A request for more work
items.explanation: Honesty has been costly, so the safe answer is the flat one.

items.prompt: A report discloses a blocker and the manager asks what would help. What does the team learn?
choices: Disclosure leads to blame
Disclosure leads to support
Disclosure changes nothing at all
items.explanation: The reaction teaches what the next disclosure will cost.

items.prompt: Where does a low-safety struggle usually end up?
choices: Being resolved early by the person alone
Being flagged by the whole team immediately
Growing quietly until a deadline is missed
items.explanation: Hidden problems keep growing.

items.prompt: Who most strongly shapes a team's psychological safety?
choices: The manager, via reactions to disclosures
Only the newest hire, through their attitude
Only the company mission statement
items.explanation: The first few reactions are the strongest lessons.

items.prompt: In a high-safety team, when does the manager typically first hear of a problem?
choices: On the morning the deadline passes
Days or weeks earlier, from the person
Only at the end of the annual review cycle
items.explanation: The person tells them early, because telling is safe.

items.prompt: A mistake is made on a low-safety team. What is the common response?
choices: Report it within the hour
Celebrate it publicly
Hide it or play it down
items.explanation: Fear of the reaction pushes it underground.

items.prompt: Is psychological safety a fixed personality trait of a team?
choices: No, it is built or eroded by responses
Yes, some teams just have it
Yes, it is fixed at the moment a team forms
items.explanation: It is built through repeated responses.

items.prompt: A manager is visibly frustrated when a report admits being behind. The report then says nothing about the next blocker. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Frustration taught that disclosure is costly, so the next one stayed hidden
The report became less capable after the first mistake and hid the next one
The next blocker was too small to mention, so staying silent was reasonable
The manager reacted correctly, so the report simply stopped needing help
items.explanation: The causal link runs from the reaction to later silence, not from the report's ability.
items.reference:
The switch
feels safe naming it: flags early, gets help
does not feel safe: hides it, finds out late
the manager's first reactions set which branch
Why: safety decides whether a visible struggle is ever reported, and it is built by how the first few disclosures are received.
items.learnMore:
Safety is built, not found

A team has high safety because of repeated experiences where honesty was met with support, not because of personalities. A manager's first reactions are the strongest of those experiences.

Common mistake

Treating safety as a fixed trait of the team that the manager cannot influence.
items.reflection: Recall a time you told someone you were stuck. What did their reaction teach you about telling them next time?

items.prompt: Two teams have identical visible signals of withdrawal. In which is the manager more likely to learn about it from the person, and why?
choices: The team with stricter deadlines, because pressure encourages candor
The team with fewer meetings, because people have more time to talk
The team with newer people, because they have not learned to hide yet
The one where earlier disclosures got support, so telling felt safe
items.explanation: The signals are equal; the willingness to report differs.

items.prompt: Which check-in is more likely to get an honest answer?
choices: 'Is everything okay with you lately?'
'You are not really being a team player, are you?'
'Your camera is off lately. What is going on?'
items.explanation: Specific and observational beats vague.

items.prompt: Why does 'everything okay?' usually get 'fine'?
choices: Nothing in it needs a specific answer
It is too aggressive to answer honestly
It asks for a written reply
items.explanation: A flat answer fits a flat question.

items.prompt: What should a specific check-in name?
choices: A guess at the cause
A change you observed
A complaint from a coworker
items.explanation: Facts seen, not conclusions drawn.

items.prompt: Where should a check-in about quiet signals happen?
choices: In the team channel
In front of the whole standup
In private, one-to-one
items.explanation: A public question adds risk to answering honestly.

items.prompt: What does a specific check-in signal to the report?
choices: The manager is paying real attention
The manager is quietly building a case on them
The manager is bored
items.explanation: Being seen supports safety.

items.prompt: Which of these is an observation, not a diagnosis?
choices: 'You are clearly burned out from this work.'
'You have not answered my last two messages.'
'You obviously do not care about this project.'
items.explanation: Observations can be checked; diagnoses invite defense.

items.prompt: After naming the change, what should the manager ask?
choices: A yes-or-no question on performance
A question about who else noticed the change
An open question about what is going on
items.explanation: Open questions give the person room to explain.

items.prompt: Does tone alone make a check-in work?
choices: No, specificity matters more than tone
Yes, a warm tone is enough
Yes, a formal tone is all that it takes here
items.explanation: Warmth helps, but 'everything okay?' stays generic in any tone.

items.prompt: A manager says, 'You seem burned out. Do you want some time off?' The report says 'no, I am fine.' What went wrong?
choices: It offered time off, which is never an appropriate thing to do
It was asked in private, which makes the report defensive
It was too specific, which gave the report too much to deny
It opened with a diagnosis, not a named, observed change
items.explanation: A diagnosis invites rejection; naming observed facts leaves room to explain.
items.reference:
Generic vs. specific
generic: 'everything okay?' invites 'yes, fine'
specific: 'your camera has been off lately' needs an answer
specific shows the manager is watching, which builds safety
Why: naming an observed change makes a flat 'fine' hard to give and shows attention, which is part of what makes honesty safe.
items.learnMore:
Observation, not accusation

A good check-in states what was seen, in neutral words, and asks an open question. It does not guess the cause or label the person.

Common mistake

Opening with a diagnosis ('you seem burned out'), which invites defense instead of explanation.
items.reflection: When did someone last ask you a specific question that made it easy to answer honestly? What made it easy?

items.prompt: Which opening is the strongest specific check-in?
choices: 'I am worried about you and want to understand what is happening. Is something going on?'
'Your performance has dropped lately. What is your plan to fix it, starting this week?'
'Your updates are shorter and two messages sat unanswered. Is something going on?'
'Some people on the team think you seem off.'
items.explanation: It names two observed changes, uses neutral words and asks an open question.

items.prompt: What should a manager do at the mild level (one signal, one week)?
choices: Start a formal process now
Announce a team-wide wellbeing review today
Note it privately and keep watching
items.explanation: Mild signals need attention, not action.

items.prompt: What response fits the moderate level?
choices: A specific private check-in
A public warning
No response at all, to avoid overreacting
items.explanation: Two or more sustained signals earn a conversation.

items.prompt: Which is a severe-level sign?
choices: One slightly shorter update
No response at all for days
A single missed optional meeting
items.explanation: Prolonged silence is a serious escalation.

items.prompt: What is the EAP?
choices: A formal performance improvement plan
A team scheduling tool
A confidential support service
items.explanation: Employee Assistance Program.

items.prompt: When is involving HR or the EAP most appropriate?
choices: At the severe level, when warranted
At the mild level, as precaution
After every moderate check-in as routine
items.explanation: Reserve escalation for the severe level.

items.prompt: What is the main mistake the framework prevents?
choices: Having too many check-ins
Having no thresholds at all
Having too much documentation on each report
items.explanation: Proportion is the point.

items.prompt: Is reacting strongly to a mild signal safe?
choices: Yes, overreaction is harmless
Yes, because mild signals are secretly severe
No, it erodes trust like ignoring does
items.explanation: Over- and under-reacting both cost trust.

items.prompt: What does the moderate level look like?
choices: Several signals together over 1 to 2 weeks
One shorter update on one day only
A formal complaint filed by the report themself
items.explanation: Several signals, sustained.

items.prompt: A manager sees a slightly shorter update, once. Which response best fits?
choices: Privately note it and keep watching
Open a formal wellbeing process
Involve HR so there is a record in place
Ask the whole team how everyone is coping
items.explanation: One signal in one week is mild; attention is enough.
items.reference:
Three levels, three responses
mild: one signal, one week: note it privately
moderate: 2+ signals, sustained: specific private check-in
severe: ignored or direct distress: immediate talk, HR or EAP
Why: matching the response to the level avoids both premature alarm and late action.
items.learnMore:
Thresholds, not hunches

A simple framework with a threshold per level keeps responses proportionate and stops every concern from being handled the same way as a task-board review.

Common mistake

Having no thresholds, so a mild signal and a severe one both get a casual 'how is the project going?'
items.reflection: Think of a worry you handled too late or too early. What threshold would have helped you choose?

items.prompt: A report has been silent for several days after a rough week and says in passing, 'I am really struggling.' Which level and response fit?
choices: Moderate: a specific check-in at the next regular one-on-one meeting
Mild: note it privately and see how the week goes
Moderate: a team-wide reminder about the support available to all
Severe: a direct, immediate talk, with HR or EAP if warranted
items.explanation: An explicit statement of distress plus prolonged silence is the severe level.

items.reference:
Three levels, three responses
mild: one signal, one week: note it privately
moderate: 2+ signals, sustained: specific private check-in
severe: ignored or direct distress: immediate talk, HR or EAP
Why: matching the response to the level avoids both premature alarm and late action.
items.learnMore:
Thresholds, not hunches

A simple framework with a threshold per level keeps responses proportionate and stops every concern from being handled the same way as a task-board review.

Common mistake

Having no thresholds, so a mild signal and a severe one both get a casual 'how is the project going?'
items.reflection: Think of a worry you handled too late or too early. What threshold would have helped you choose?
